quiz.question: What does a successful write() system call guarantee by itself on Linux?
options: The data is safely stored on persistent physical flash/magnetic media
The kernel accepted the bytes into memory (e.g. page cache), unless an error was returned
The directory entry and file name have been synchronized to non-volatile storage
The file update is guaranteed crash-consistent across power loss
quiz.explanation: A successful write() merely confirms that the operating system kernel accepted the bytes into volatile memory (the page cache). It does NOT guarantee that data has been flushed to persistent storage media.

quiz.question: In a crash-safe file replacement protocol, why must you synchronize the temporary file (fsync) before calling rename()?
options: To prevent other concurrent processes from opening the containing directory
To ensure the complete new file contents and inode metadata are durable on disk before publishing the new name
To disable filesystem journal transactions during the update
To force the Linux virtual memory manager to evict the page cache
quiz.explanation: If you rename before fsync(), a sudden crash can leave the new directory entry pointing to unwritten, empty, or garbage blocks on disk. Synchronizing first ensures that the contents are durable before the namespace pointer is switched.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of performing fsync() on the containing directory descriptor after an atomic rename?
options: To synchronize the directory-entry change (dentry namespace link) to persistent storage
To recalculate SHA-256 checksums for every file in the directory
To purge all inactive file buffers from RAM
To allow the rename syscall to work across different filesystems
quiz.explanation: Directories are themselves files containing directory entries (dentries). While rename() is atomic in RAM, calling fsync() on the directory file descriptor requests that the directory block update is flushed to persistent storage.

quiz.question: What does filesystem journaling (such as in ext4 or XFS) primarily protect?
options: It guarantees that every multi-file application transaction is ACID-compliant
It allows the filesystem to quickly restore structural consistency (inodes, bitmaps, directory trees) after a crash
It eliminates the possibility of physical storage hardware degradation
It eliminates the need for periodic backups
quiz.explanation: Journaling protects filesystem structural invariants (free lists, inode tables, directory links) so that the filesystem can mount quickly without a lengthy fsck scan. It does NOT automatically make application-level business transactions consistent.

quiz.question: Why is an active restore drill an indispensable part of a production backup strategy?
options: It guarantees that data will never be corrupted in the future
It verifies that the backup files can actually be restored into working, consistent application state
It replaces the need for filesystem checksums and RAID arrays
It automatically reduces the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) to zero seconds
quiz.explanation: Untested backups frequently fail due to missing encryption keys, incompatible database versions, corrupted media, or missing configuration files. A backup is only as good as a proven, successful restore drill.

quiz.question: What is the primary limitation of simulated crash testing that uses process exceptions or signal kills?
options: It cannot model application-level state transitions
It does not reproduce real storage-controller cache loss, power failure, or kernel writeback reordering
It is unable to compute cryptographic hashes like SHA-256
It requires a raw unpartitioned NVMe drive to run
quiz.explanation: An exception or process kill leaves the operating system kernel and hardware running, allowing dirty page cache pages to be flushed normally. Real power loss stops the CPU immediately, exposing volatile cache data loss and device reordering.

theorySections.title: 1. Volatile versus Persistent State
paragraphs: RAM · Page Cache · Disk Controller Caches · Durability Boundaries · ACID Terminology
A successful write call does not mean your data has reached non-volatile storage media. When you call write() in Python or C, bytes travel through multiple caching layers:
C runtime FILE* or language buffer (e.g. 4KB). Lost on process crash.
OS dirty memory pages awaiting flusher threads. Lost on power failure or kernel panic.
On-drive volatile buffer inside SSD controller. Lost unless battery/capacitor backed (PLP).
Non-volatile floating-gate/charge-trap cells. Survives power disconnection.
An update appears to take effect as a single indivisible step. Readers never observe an intermediate half-written state. (e.g. rename()).
System rules and business logic remain valid before and after recovery (e.g. Account Balance matches Ledger history, directory dentries match inodes).
Once acknowledged as durable, committed data survives power cuts, kernel panics, and reboots under the hardware durability contract.

theorySections.title: 2. Write Ordering, Barriers, and fsync()
paragraphs: write() vs fflush() vs close() vs fsync() vs fdatasync() · Flushes & Barriers · FUA
To enforce durability, operating systems expose explicit synchronization primitives:

Computers and flash controllers reorder writes for performance. If you write new file data, rename it into a directory, and power fails before the file data is flushed, the directory entry will point to uninitialized garbage or zero-filled blocks! You must issue a barrier: fsync(file) BEFORE rename().
Step through T0 to T4 to observe where data resides, what callers see, and when true durability across power failure is reached.

theorySections.title: 3. Journaling and Copy-on-Write (CoW) Filesystems
paragraphs: ext4 & XFS vs Btrfs & ZFS · Metadata consistency · Atomic tree roots · Write amplification
Modern filesystems employ one of two architectural paradigms to ensure that sudden crashes leave the on-disk structures recoverable without a multi-hour fsck scan:

Logs metadata operations to a circular write-ahead log (journal) on disk before updating home blocks. On reboot, the kernel inspects the journal and replays committed transactions or discards incomplete ones.
Never overwrites existing data blocks in-place! Writes modified data and metadata out-of-place to fresh blocks, then atomically updates parent tree pointers up to the superblock root.
Compare step-by-step how ext4 Journaling updates metadata versus how Btrfs/ZFS Copy-on-Write flips root pointers.

paragraphs: The unsafe truncation bug · Staged temporary files · os.replace() · Directory synchronization
Consider the naive file update pattern taught in introductory programming courses:
Opening in "w" mode truncates the file immediately. If power fails or the process dies during serialization, your previous valid configuration is destroyed and replaced with a corrupt 0-byte file.

theorySections.title: 5. Crash Windows and Recovery Invariants
paragraphs: Crash window analysis · Write-ahead logs (WAL) · Idempotent recovery · Checksum validation
A crash consistency analysis asks a rigorous question: "If execution cuts out at instruction $N$, what state will be found on disk when the system powers back on?"
If the recovery procedure itself crashes midway, executing it again on the next reboot must not corrupt data.
A transaction is either committed or discarded. Never infer completion from partial data presence alone.
Validate payloads against expected checksums to detect silent block bit-rot and partial sector overwrites.
Inject sudden power failure at different checkpoints during a file update. Inspect what survives after reboot and what recovery must do.

paragraphs: RPO & RTO · Backup failure modes · Disaster recovery drills · Cryptographic verification
A backup is meaningless unless you can prove that it can be restored into a functioning, consistent production environment.
The maximum acceptable data loss measured backwards in time. An RPO of 15 minutes means transactions older than 15 minutes must never be lost.
The maximum acceptable duration of service downtime from initial disaster declaration until the restored service passes production health checks.
